input:
Liquid-liquid extraction, in chemical separations, serves as a widely utilised and highly effective technique for recovering valuable compounds from process streams. In this case, the technique is applied to the recovery of phenol from an aqueous stream, with the phenol being transferred into an organic solvent phase. A key parameter that plays a crucial role in governing the separation is the distribution coefficient, defined as the ratio between the concentration in the organic phase and the concentration in the aqueous phase. This coefficient has a value of 1.58 at a temperature of 25 °C, indicating that phenol preferentially partitions into the organic phase, thereby facilitating efficient recovery. The design of the extraction unit is based on the use of 8 countercurrent stages, which work together to maximise contact between the two phases, ensuring thorough transfer throughout the cascade. On this design, the predicted recovery is an impressive 93% of the phenol contained in the feed.

It is important to note that this prediction rests on simplifying assumptions not yet validated. Firstly, every stage is assumed to behave as a perfect equilibrium stage, and secondly, the mutual solubility of the two solvents is assumed to be negligible, which together allow the calculations to proceed in a straightforward manner. Neither assumption has been checked against the real solvents involved, highlighting a significant gap between the idealised model and the physical system. Should real stages fall short of equilibrium, or should the solvents prove appreciably mutually soluble, the recovery achieved with 8 stages could potentially fall below the predicted 93%. Furthermore, the distribution coefficient is only a single value at 25 °C, so operation at another temperature would shift the equilibrium and the recovery the unit can deliver.
target:
Liquid-liquid extraction recovers phenol from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, the ratio of the phenol concentration in the organic phase to that in the aqueous phase, is 1.58 at 25 °C. A coefficient above unity means phenol favours the organic phase at equilibrium, and a countercurrent cascade repeats the contact so that the transfer accumulates stage by stage. The design uses 8 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 93% of the phenol in the feed.

The prediction rests on two assumptions. Each stage is treated as an equilibrium stage, with the leaving streams at their equilibrium compositions. Mutual solubility of the two solvents is neglected, with each phase treated as solvent and phenol only, so the phase flow rates stay constant along the cascade. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents: no stage-efficiency measurement and no mutual-solubility data for the solvent pair in use stand behind the design. The recovery figure is a prediction under idealised contacting, not a measured performance. If the actual stages fall short of equilibrium, or if the two solvents dissolve appreciably in each other, the recovery at 8 stages falls below 93%. The distribution coefficient is a single value at 25 °C; operation at another temperature changes the equilibrium, and the recovery changes with it.
